Welcome. This chapter covers how networks are built, how data moves, and how we keep it safe. Point out the ☰ Contents button and the dotted words, which show definitions.

OBJECTIVES

  • Types, characteristics and uses of networks.
  • Network components and network servers.
  • Cloud computing and data transmission.
  • Network protocols, addressing and routing.
  • Wireless technology and mobile communications.
  • Network security threats and prevention.
  • Disaster-recovery management.
  • Advantages and disadvantages of each.
2
Read the objectives aloud. Ask: which networks have you already used today? (Home Wi-Fi, mobile data, school LAN.)

14.1 Types of Network

  • Network: devices (nodes) connected to share data.
  • Also shares peripherals, storage and internet access.
  • Types:
  • Local area network (LAN)
  • Wide area network (WAN)
  • Client-server and peer-to-peer
  • Virtual private network (VPN)
  • Mobile (cellular) network
3
A network is any set of nodes sharing data. Quick poll: which of these types has each student used this week? A VPN may surprise them.

14.1 Local Area Network
(LAN)

  • Internal network for one site or organisation.
  • E.g. a school, home or office.
  • Covers a small area, a few kilometres.
  • Can transfer hundreds of Gbit/s.
  • Uses Ethernet (wired) and Wi-Fi (wireless).
  • Works at OSI layers 1 and 2.
  • Cheap and easy to install and extend.
  • Several LANs can form a MAN, e.g. a city.
4
Stress “one site or organisation”. LANs are fast because distances are short. A MAN is just several LANs across a city.

14.1 LAN: Evaluation

Advantages

  • Fewer peripherals needed, so lower costs.
  • Files and templates stored centrally.
  • Central backups and access control.
  • One shared internet connection and IP address.
  • Software updates rolled out centrally.

Disadvantages

  • Covers only a small area.
  • Needs a network administrator.
  • Malware spreads easily between devices.
5
Green items are advantages and red items are disadvantages. Exam tip: “evaluate” questions need both, with a conclusion.

14.1 Wide Area Network
(WAN)

  • Covers a large area: cities or countries.
  • Connects distant LANs together.
  • Uses public or leased telecoms lines.
  • Not owned by one organisation.
  • The internet is the largest WAN.
  • Store and forward: data stored at each node.
  • Slower than a LAN, about 150–200 Mbit/s.
  • More errors and delays over long distances.
6
Store and forward: each node holds the data before passing it on, which adds delay. Ask why a WAN is slower and has more errors than a LAN.

14.1 WAN Protocols

  • High-Level Data Link Control (HDLC):
  • Routers repackage LAN packets for leased lines.
  • Provides error correction.
  • PPP: based on HDLC, for dial-up links.
  • Frame relay:
  • Variable-size frames over public networks.
  • No error correction, so less reliable.
  • Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS): short labels speed up routing.
7
Students only need to recognise these: HDLC has error correction, frame relay does not, and MPLS speeds up routing with labels.

14.1 WAN: Evaluation

Advantages

  • Resources centralised at head office.
  • Staff access resources from any site.
  • Leased lines keep data private.
  • Cheaper calls and video conferences (VoIP).

Disadvantages

  • High set-up costs over long distances.
  • Remote sites may be less secure.
  • Data centre must run 24/7.
  • Leased lines are expensive to maintain.
8
Link to the school: how could a group of schools share resources over a WAN? Leased lines are private but expensive.

14.1 Client-Server Networks

  • Clients request services from servers.
  • Server waits, then sends a response.
  • Request-response model.
  • Clients do not share their resources.
  • Low-power clients use powerful servers.
  • Connections made only when needed.
  • E.g. web browsing, email, printing, file storage.
  • Too many requests can cause denial of service.
9
Request-response model. Analogy: a restaurant, where customers (clients) order and the kitchen (server) responds. Too many orders means denial of service.

14.1 Client-Server:
Evaluation

Advantages

  • Central control of access rights.
  • Files stored and found in one place.
  • Central backups; users needn’t do them.
  • Updates rolled out from one place.

Disadvantages

  • Server failure stops everyone.
  • Expensive servers and skilled technicians.
  • Heavy traffic can cause congestion.
10
Key exam point: a single point of failure. If the server goes down, every client is affected.

14.1 Peer-to-Peer Networks

  • Nodes connect as equals, with no central server.
  • Peers share files, storage, bandwidth and processing.
  • A form of distributed computing.
  • Unstructured: connections made when needed.
  • Structured: a distributed hash table (DHT) maps nodes.
  • Nodes can join and leave freely.
  • E.g. file sharing, Bitcoin, Apple AirDrop.
11
No central server: every peer is both client and server. Ask for examples students know, e.g. AirDrop.

14.1 BitTorrent

  • P2P protocol for transferring large files.
  • File split into pieces held by many peers.
  • Peers sharing the file form a swarm.
  • Seeds hold the complete file.
  • Pieces downloaded from many peers at once.
  • Pieces reassembled into the complete file.
  • Trackers, now a DHT, locate the peers.
  • Faster and less bandwidth than FTP or HTTP.
12
Introduce the swarm, seeds and pieces. The next slide lets them see why downloading from many peers is faster.

14.1 BitTorrent

Why is downloading from a swarm faster?The file is split into pieces, and different peers send you different pieces at the same time.


The seed has the whole file. Other peers have some pieces. Each colour shows which peer sent that piece.

Press a button to download the same 24-piece file.
Try it
Run “one server” first, then the swarm with 1, 4 and 8 peers. Ask: why does the 1-peer swarm take as long as the server? Point out the coloured pieces arriving from different peers.

14.1 Peer-to-Peer:
Evaluation

Advantages

  • Cheap: no central server needed.
  • Quick to set up with little configuration.
  • Removing a node doesn’t affect others.
  • No central record, so more privacy.

Disadvantages

  • Each device manages its own security.
  • No central backups.
  • Illegal file sharing is hard to stop.
  • Shared files can carry malware.
13
Balance: cheap and private, but no central security or backups. Mention legal issues with sharing copyrighted files.

14.1 Virtual Private Network
(VPN)

  • Connects to a private LAN over public networks.
  • Remote users appear to be on the LAN.
  • Point-to-point connection between two nodes.
  • Traffic is sent via a VPN server.
  • User’s IP address is hidden.
  • Uses tunneling, encryption and authentication.
  • Protocols: L2TP, IPsec and TLS.
14
A VPN makes a remote user appear to be on the LAN. Tunneling plus encryption plus authentication. Ask who uses one and why.

14.1 VPN: Uses &
Evaluation

  • Staff work securely from home.
  • Secure use of public Wi-Fi hotspots.
  • Avoids geo-restrictions and censorship.

Advantages

  • Encryption keeps data private.
  • Cheaper than leased lines.

Disadvantages

  • Slower: traffic passes through VPN servers.
  • Providers may log and sell user data.
  • Illegal in some countries.
15
Uses first, then evaluation. Discuss: why might VPNs be illegal in some countries?

14.1 Mobile Networks

  • Wireless network made of cells.
  • Each cell has a base station.
  • Neighbouring cells use different frequencies.
  • Frequencies reused in non-adjacent cells.
  • Handoff passes calls between base stations.
  • Lower frequency: larger range, less data.
  • Higher frequency: more capacity, short range.
  • 2G/3G use GPRS; 4G/5G use IP.
16
Cells, base stations and frequency reuse. The interactive version comes later, in 14.8. Lower frequency means more range but less data.

14.1 Mobile Networks:
Evaluation

Advantages

  • Calls, data and internet on the move.
  • Contactless payments anywhere.
  • Staff work while travelling.
  • Delivery vehicles tracked via GPS and mobile data.

Disadvantages

  • Wireless data can be intercepted.
  • Calls and data can be expensive.
  • Poor coverage in rural areas and tunnels.
17
Ask students to give one advantage and one disadvantage of mobile networks from their own experience, e.g. no signal in tunnels.

14.1 Tunneling

  • Wraps (encapsulates) packets inside other packets.
  • Moves private data over public networks.
  • Carries ‘foreign’ protocols over a network.
  • 1 Packet wrapped in a tunneling packet.
  • 2 Sent across the public network.
  • 3 Unwrapped at the destination LAN.
  • E.g. IPv6 packets carried over IPv4 networks.
  • Used to create VPNs.
18
Tunneling: a packet inside a packet, like posting a sealed letter inside another envelope. It is the basis of VPNs.

14.1 Architecture &
Topology

  • Architecture: the network’s overall design:
  • Hardware, e.g. routers, gateways, user devices.
  • Transmission media, wired and wireless.
  • Protocols, services and topology.
  • E.g. client-server or peer-to-peer.
  • Topology: how nodes and links are arranged.
  • Physical: actual layout of cables and devices.
  • Logical: the path data travels.
19
Architecture is the whole design. Topology is just the layout. Physical layout is the cables; logical layout is the path the data takes.

14.1 Physical Topologies

  • Star: all nodes connect to a central switch.
  • One cable fails, only one node affected.
  • Bus: nodes share one main cable.
  • Cheap, but collisions and cable failure.
  • Ring: each node joined to the next.
  • Data travels round in one direction.
  • Mesh: nodes link to many others.
  • Many routes, so very robust; e.g. the internet.
20
Go through all four topologies, then use the next slide to break cables and test each one.

14.1 Physical Topologies

What happens when a cable breaks?Tap a cable to cut it, then send a packet. Tap a computer to change where it goes.

Star

Try it
Start with star: cut one cable and send to that computer, then to another. Bus: cut the backbone and the whole bus fails. Ring: send A→F to see the long way round. Mesh: cut several cables until it fails.

14.1 Uses of Networks

  • Sharing and storing resources and files.
  • Sharing peripherals, e.g. printers.
  • Exchanging data, e.g. email and messaging.
  • BitTorrent for transferring large files.
  • Access to internet services.
  • Tunneling between private networks.
  • Telephony, e.g. VoIP calls.
  • Content delivery: streaming and software downloads.
21
Recap the uses. Ask students to match each use to a network type from this section.

14.2 Network Components

  • Hardware needed to build a network.
  • Connect devices into a network:
  • NICs and WNICs
  • Repeaters, hubs and switches
  • Wireless access points
  • Connect networks together:
  • Bridges and gateways
  • Routers and firewalls
24
Two groups: devices that connect devices into a network, and devices that connect networks together. The rest of 14.2 goes through each one.

14.2 Network Interface Card
(NIC)

  • Connects a device to the transmission medium.
  • Often built into the motherboard.
  • Has a unique MAC address set in manufacture.
  • Converts parallel CPU data into serial frames.
  • Sends frames as electrical, light or radio signals.
  • Reads every frame on the medium.
  • Keeps frames with its own MAC address.
  • Checks frames with a checksum.
25
Every NIC has a MAC address set during manufacture. It converts parallel data to serial frames and back.

14.2 Wireless NIC (WNIC)

  • Connects a device to a radio network.
  • Used for Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and mobile networks.
  • Has its own unique MAC address.
  • Modulates data onto radio carrier waves.
  • Handles errors and frequent retries.
  • Two modes:
  • Ad hoc: devices connect directly, peer-to-peer.
  • Infrastructure: devices connect through a WAP.
26
Ad hoc: devices connect directly. Infrastructure: devices connect via a WAP. Ask which mode a home network uses.

14.2 Repeaters

  • Signals weaken over distance.
  • Repeater receives and regenerates the signal.
  • Extends the range of a network.
  • Works only at the Physical layer.
  • Fibre repeaters can amplify light directly.
  • Wi-Fi extenders repeat wireless signals.
  • Extenders can halve bandwidth.
  • Extenders add interference and reduce security.
27
Signals weaken over distance, so a repeater regenerates them. Wi-Fi extenders are repeaters, but they can halve the bandwidth.

14.2 Hubs

  • Multi-port repeater.
  • Connects several devices in a star.
  • Sends every frame to all other ports.
  • Cannot tell which port a frame is for.
  • Works at the Physical layer.
  • Many collisions, so slow network.
  • Frames can be captured, a security risk.
  • Now replaced by switches.
28
A hub is a multi-port repeater: it cannot read addresses, so every frame goes everywhere. That causes collisions and lets frames be captured.

14.2 Switches

  • Connects devices within a LAN.
  • Reads the destination MAC address.
  • Keeps a table of MAC addresses per port.
  • Sends frames only to the correct port.
  • Unknown address: frame sent to all ports.
  • Less traffic and fewer collisions than a hub.
  • Works at the Data Link layer (layer 2).
  • Can split a large LAN into segments.
29
A switch learns MAC addresses. An unknown address is sent to all ports at first, then it learns. Demonstrate on the next slide.

14.2 Hubs & Switches

Hub or switch: who receives the frame?Tap a sender, then a receiver. Then try sending three frames at once.

Hub

MAC address table
Frames carried on cables0
Try it
Hub mode: send A→D and count the frames on the cables, then press “three at once” to cause a collision. Switch mode: send A→D (flooded), then D→A (direct, because it has learned). Compare the frame counts.

14.2 Types of Switch

  • Unmanaged: no configuration; small LANs.
  • Smart: limited settings via a web page.
  • Managed: fully configured by an administrator.
  • Managed switches can create VLANs.
  • They can prioritise types of traffic.
  • Port mirroring copies frames for analysis.
  • Used for intruder detection and packet sniffing.
  • Layer 3 switches can act as routers.
30
Unmanaged, smart and managed switches. VLANs and port mirroring are on managed switches. Layer 3 switches blur the line with routers.

14.2 Wireless Access Point
(WAP)

  • Connects wireless devices to a wired network.
  • Contains a WNIC to provide Wi-Fi.
  • Sends beacon frames with the network’s SSID.
  • Devices scan for beacons and list networks.
  • Asks for a passphrase to connect.
  • Passphrase generates encryption keys (WPA2/WPA3).
  • Connected devices share its bandwidth.
  • Often built into home routers.
31
The WAP broadcasts beacon frames with the SSID. The passphrase generates the encryption keys. All connected devices share its bandwidth.

14.2 Gateways & Bridges

  • Gateway:
  • Joins networks that use different protocols.
  • Translates between the protocols.
  • Default gateway receives unknown destinations.
  • Network address translation (NAT) shares one IP.
  • Bridge:
  • Joins segments of a LAN, e.g. two buildings.
  • Uses a MAC address table to forward frames.
32
Gateway: translates between protocols. Bridge: joins LAN segments. NAT lets a whole home share one public IP address.

14.2 Routers

  • Connects different networks, e.g. LAN to internet.
  • Reads the destination IP address.
  • Looks up a route in its routing table.
  • Forwards packets from router to router.
  • Unknown destination: sent to a default router.
  • Time to live (TTL) drops at each hop.
  • Packet discarded when TTL reaches zero.
  • Works at the Network layer (layer 3).
33
Routers read IP addresses and use routing tables. TTL drops at each hop, which stops packets looping forever.

14.2 Switch vs Router

  • Similarities:
  • Both forward data using store and forward.
  • Both use address tables.
  • Differences:
  • Switch: within one network; router: between networks.
  • Switch uses MAC addresses; router uses IP.
  • Switch: layer 2; router: layer 3.
  • Routers adapt routes and can perform NAT.
34
Classic exam comparison. Get students to write a three-row table: scope, address type, layer.

14.2 Components Working
Together

  • 1 Laptop’s NIC sends request frames.
  • 2 WAP or switch passes them on.
  • 3 Unknown address, so sent to the gateway.
  • 4 Router forwards them to the ISP.
  • 5 Routers pass them to the web server.
  • 6 Reply returns the same way.
  • Delay along the path is called latency.
  • Streaming uses a buffer to hide latency.
35
Walk through the journey of a web request. Latency builds up at each step, and buffers hide it when streaming.

14.3 Network Servers

  • Node that provides services to clients.
  • Fast CPUs, large RAM and fast storage.
  • Often rack-mounted in data centres.
  • Centralise resources, services and security.
  • Types:
  • File, web, mail and applications servers
  • Print, FTP and proxy servers
  • Virtual servers
38
Servers provide services to clients. Data centres hold racks of them. Preview the types covered in this section.

14.3 Request and Response

  • Basis of client-server communication.
  • 1 Client sends a request.
  • 2 Server is listening, e.g. on port 80.
  • 3 Server processes it and sends a response.
  • 4 Client makes further requests.
  • 5 Repeats until all data is sent.
  • E.g. a web page needs many requests.
  • Server shares resources; client does not.
39
One web page can need dozens of requests: HTML, images, scripts. Port 80 is HTTP.

14.3 File Server

  • Stores files and folders for users.
  • Users store and retrieve files from any client.
  • Network-attached storage (NAS) is a modern form.
  • Large, cheap magnetic hard disks.
  • RAID spreads files across several disks.
  • Login and access rights protect files.
  • Appears to users as a network drive.
  • Usually on a LAN, unlike cloud storage.
40
A file server appears as a network drive. RAID spreads data over several disks. Contrast it with cloud storage.

14.3 Web Server

  • Stores websites and sends their content.
  • Browser requests pages using HTTP or HTTPS.
  • Server finds the resource by its URL.
  • Status codes: 200 OK, 404 Not Found.
  • Server-side scripts create dynamic pages.
  • Faster, and source code stays hidden.
  • Printers and routers have embedded web servers.
41
Status codes: 200 OK and 404 Not Found. Server-side scripts build dynamic pages, and the source code stays hidden.

14.3 Mail Server

  • Receives, stores and forwards email.
  • Client sends mail to the server using SMTP.
  • Server finds the recipient’s server using DNS.
  • Message waits in the recipient’s inbox.
  • Client collects it with POP3 or IMAP.
  • POP3: moves mail to one device.
  • IMAP: copies mail; stays on the server.
  • Own mail server needs skill to fight spam.
42
SMTP sends. POP3 moves mail to one device. IMAP keeps it on the server for all your devices. Ask which your phone uses.

14.3 Applications & Print
Servers

  • Applications server:
  • Runs applications; clients use a browser.
  • No installation on clients.
  • Same software version for all staff.
  • Print server:
  • Queues jobs and sends them to printers.
  • Manages, reorders and audits print jobs.
  • User may not see printer errors.
43
An applications server means nothing to install on each client. A print server queues and audits print jobs.

14.3 FTP Server

  • Stores files accessed with File Transfer Protocol.
  • User logs in, or connects anonymously.
  • Separate connections for control and data.
  • Used to distribute software and documents.
  • Use FTPS or a VPN for security.

Advantages

  • Simple and standard on all systems.

Disadvantages

  • Logins and data not encrypted.
  • Firewalls may block or drop connections.
44
FTP is simple but unencrypted. Use FTPS or a VPN. Separate control and data connections can confuse firewalls.

14.3 Proxy Server

  • Go-between for clients and other servers.
  • Intercepts and checks requests and responses.
  • Replaces the client’s IP address with its own.
  • Schools use it to filter content.
  • Caches popular pages for faster access.
  • Reverse proxy shares load between web servers.
  • Can become a bottleneck.
  • Can break FTP and VoIP connections.
45
Proxy: a go-between that filters (like the school filter), caches and hides the client IP. A reverse proxy balances load.

14.3 Virtual Server

  • Software instance of a server.
  • Many run on one physical machine.
  • Each has its own OS and server software.
  • Managed remotely; e.g. web hosting.

Advantages

  • Saves power, space and hardware costs.
  • Quickly moved to another machine.

Disadvantages

  • Host failure stops all virtual servers.
  • Data could leak between virtual servers.
46
Many virtual servers run on one machine. This saves power and space, but a host failure stops all of them.

14.3 Server Farms

  • Many servers networked to act as one.
  • Can contain thousands of servers.
  • A central server schedules and shares tasks.
  • Balances the load between servers.
  • Very fast for large tasks.
  • Basis of data centres and supercomputers.
  • Huge power and cooling needs.
  • DHCP servers also assign IP addresses.
47
Server farms act as one big computer with load balancing. Mention the huge power and cooling needs.

14.3 Servers: Evaluation

Advantages

  • Resources centralised and backed up.
  • Clients added without reconfiguring.
  • Central security rules and access rights.
  • Cheaper than many standalone workstations.

Disadvantages

  • Too many requests reduce performance.
  • Server failure stops its clients.
  • Expensive to install and administer.
  • Web hosts control the business’s data.
48
Evaluation summary. Ask: for a small business, are servers worth it? Justify.

14.4 Cloud Computing

  • Sharing computing resources over a network.
  • Storage, servers, databases and processing power.
  • Resources spread across data centres.
  • Available on demand over the internet.
  • Works on any type of device.
  • Resources scale up or down as needed.
  • Users kept logically separate.
  • Use is monitored and billed.
51
Cloud = someone else’s computers, on demand. Ask which cloud services students use, e.g. Google Drive.

14.4 Cloud Service Models

  • Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS):
  • Virtual machines, e.g. for testing or backup.
  • Platform as a Service (PaaS):
  • OS and tools for developers.
  • Software as a Service (SaaS):
  • Applications run in a web browser.
  • Private cloud: on the organisation’s own network.
  • Public cloud: third party; hybrid: both.
52
IaaS, PaaS and SaaS: the next slide shows who manages what. Private, public and hybrid describe where the cloud runs.

14.4 Cloud Service Models

Who manages what?Tap a model. Red is what you manage; grey is what the cloud provider manages.

of 9 layers managed by you
You manageProvider manages
Try it
Tap each model in turn and count the red layers: 9, 5, 2, 0. Ask: which model would a developer want? Which would a small shop want?

14.4 Uses of Cloud
Computing

  • Individuals:
  • File storage, e.g. Google Drive, Dropbox.
  • Files synchronised across devices.
  • Streaming, gaming, email and social media.
  • Organisations:
  • Staff access resources from anywhere.
  • Real-time collaboration on documents.
  • Rent only the resources needed.
53
Individuals vs organisations. Real-time collaboration: these slides are themselves a web app.

14.4 Cloud: Advantages

  • No hardware to buy or maintain.
  • Automatic backups and updates.
  • Very large storage capacity.
  • Access from any device, anywhere.
  • Scale up quickly, e.g. during a sale.
  • Fewer IT staff needed.
  • Lower energy, heating and cooling costs.
54
Seven advantages. Ask students to rank the top three for a school.

14.4 Cloud: Disadvantages

  • Needs a reliable internet connection.
  • Ongoing subscription costs.
  • Security is controlled by the provider.
  • Locked in to one supplier.
  • Data lost if the provider fails.
  • Attacks on shared servers affect many firms.
  • Data may fall under several countries’ laws.
55
Now the disadvantages. Debate: should the school move everything to the cloud?

14.5 Bandwidth & Bit Rate

  • Data sent as signals along a medium.
  • Guided media: copper and fibre cables.
  • Unguided media: wireless and lasers.
  • Bandwidth: maximum rate of data transfer.
  • Bit rate: bits actually transferred per second.
  • Measured in bit/s, e.g. kbit/s, Mbit/s.
  • Bit rate cannot exceed the bandwidth.
  • E.g. 100 Mbit/s network, video at 75 Mbit/s.
58
Bandwidth is the maximum and bit rate is the actual. Analogy: a motorway’s capacity vs the cars actually on it.

14.5 Bandwidth of Media

  • Ethernet: up to 400 Gbit/s.
  • Fibre: 1 Gbit/s single mode; up to 40 Gbit/s multi-mode.
  • Twisted pair: 100 Mbit/s to 1 Gbit/s.
  • Coaxial LANs: only 10 Mbit/s.
  • Wi-Fi: 54 Mbit/s up to about 1 Gbit/s.
  • Bluetooth: about 1–3 Mbit/s.
  • Mobile: 3G 5 Mbit/s; 4G up to 1 Gbit/s.
  • 5G: 10 Gbit/s or more promised.
59
Compare the media. Ask students to predict before the race on the next slide.

14.5 Bandwidth of Media

How long would the download take?Choose a file, predict the winner, then race the media. Tap a row to see the working.

4 GB
Simulated time0 s
Time = file size in bits ÷ bit rate. Best-case speeds from the notes; real bit rates are lower. 1 GB = 1000 MB here.
Try it
Choose “HD film 4 GB” and ask for predictions before racing. Then tap Wi-Fi to show the working: size × 8 ÷ bit rate. Repeat with the 80 GB game.

14.5 Data Streaming

  • Media plays before it is fully downloaded.
  • Data stored first in a buffer.
  • Buffer covers short gaps in the connection.
  • Buffer empties, so video freezes.
  • Real-time: live events, e.g. sport, concerts.
  • On-demand: pre-recorded, e.g. films.
  • Also continuous data, e.g. stock exchanges.
  • Content is compressed to reduce bandwidth.
60
The buffer is the key idea: it covers short gaps in the connection. Real-time streaming (live sport) vs on-demand (films).

14.5 Bit Rate & Streaming
Quality

  • Higher bit rate gives better quality.
  • Low bit rate: jerky, pixelated video.
  • Audio drop-outs and ‘warbling’ sounds.
  • SD video needs about 2 Mbit/s.
  • HD needs about 5 Mbit/s.
  • UHD needs about 25 Mbit/s.
  • Audio bit rate = sample rate × bits × channels.
  • Bandwidth must exceed the stream’s bit rate.
61
Bit rate sets the quality: SD 2, HD 5, UHD 25 Mbit/s. The bandwidth must be more than the stream’s bit rate.

14.5 Bit Rate & Streaming

Why does a video freeze?Change the bandwidth and the video quality. Watch the buffer.

Buffering…
HD
0:00
Buffer
0.0 s

Video quality (bit rate)
Freezes0
Try it
Start at 8 Mbit/s on HD: it plays smoothly. Drop to 3 Mbit/s and it freezes. Switch to SD and it recovers. Try UHD at 8 Mbit/s. Use “connection drops” to show the buffer covering a gap.

14.5 Fibre-Optic Cable

  • Thin strands of glass or plastic.
  • Data carried as pulses of light.
  • Total internal reflection keeps light in the core.
  • Lasers or LEDs create the light.
  • Many wavelengths carry separate channels.
  • Single mode: one wavelength; multi-mode: many.
  • Used for long-distance and international links.
  • Repeaters boost light over long distances.
62
Light in glass, kept in by total internal reflection. Many wavelengths give many channels.

14.5 Fibre-Optic Cable

How does light stay inside the fibre?Change the angle of the laser. If the light hits the boundary at more than the critical angle, it is totally internally reflected.


Angle at the boundary
Critical angle69°

Core: glass, refractive index 1.50. Cladding: 1.40. Angles are measured from the normal (dashed line).

Try it
Start at a small angle: total internal reflection. Increase the angle until the light escapes (boundary angle below 69°). Send pulses in both cases and compare what the detector receives.

14.5 Fibre Optic: Evaluation

Advantages

  • Very high bandwidth over long distances.
  • No electromagnetic interference.
  • Hard to tap, so secure.
  • Light, thin and resists corrosion.

Disadvantages

  • Snaps if bent too sharply.
  • Joins need skilled technicians.
  • Long-distance repeaters are expensive.
63
Fibre evaluation. Ask: why do undersea cables use fibre?

14.5 Copper Cables

  • Coaxial:
  • Copper core inside a braided shield.
  • Used for cable and satellite TV.
  • Twisted pair:
  • Twists cancel interference and crosstalk.
  • UTP or shielded STP; e.g. Cat 5e.

Advantages

  • Cheap, well shielded, little maintenance.

Disadvantages

  • Too little bandwidth for modern LANs.
64
Coaxial is used for TV. Twisted pair is used for Ethernet: the twists cancel interference.

14.5 Twisted Pair:
Evaluation

  • Used for telephone lines and Ethernet LANs.
  • Maximum length about 100 m.
  • RJ45 connectors.

Advantages

  • High bandwidth, up to 1 Gbit/s.
  • Cheap and easy to install.

Disadvantages

  • More interference than fibre.
  • Damaged by kinks and sharp bends.
  • Plastic coating is a fire risk.
65
Maximum about 100 m. RJ45 connectors. Cheap, but more interference than fibre.

14.5 Lasers

  • Send data through free space: air or space.
  • Infrared light; needs line of sight.
  • Must be aimed very accurately.
  • About 500 m range in the atmosphere.
  • Used between buildings, satellites and spacecraft.

Advantages

  • High bandwidth; hard to eavesdrop.

Disadvantages

  • Blocked by dust, rain and obstacles.
  • Expensive and can damage eyes.
66
Free-space lasers need precise aim and line of sight. Weather blocks them.

14.5 Effect of the Medium

  • Bandwidth depends on the number of signals.
  • Also on the modulation method used.
  • Mixed media reduce available bandwidth.
  • Fibre and twisted pair give the highest bandwidth.
  • Streaming needs high, steady bandwidth.
  • UHD TV needs about 25 Mbit/s.
  • Only high-bandwidth media carry UHD.
67
Bandwidth depends on the medium and the modulation. UHD needs about 25 Mbit/s, so only high-bandwidth media can carry it.

14.5 Mind Map

Data transmission: the big pictureTap a branch to focus on it. Tap ↗ to jump to that slide.

Summary
Use this to recap the section. Ask students to explain one branch each, or tap a branch to jump back to its slide.

14.5 Quick Quiz

Quiz
Quick check. The streaming and fibre interactives make good hints if students get stuck.

PAST PAPERSMARK SCHEME

68–69
Give students a few minutes to answer, then press Reveal mark scheme and self-mark.

14.6 Network Protocols

  • Protocol: agreed rules for communication.
  • Protocols set out how devices:
  • Identify themselves
  • Create connections
  • Package the data
  • Route data between devices
  • Devices must use the same protocols.
  • Most networks use the TCP/IP suite.
70
A protocol is an agreed set of rules. Analogy: the rules of a language or a sport. Devices must use the same protocols.

14.6 Reliable & Unreliable
Protocols

  • Reliable:
  • Tells the sender whether data arrived.
  • Used when data must arrive, e.g. logins.
  • E.g. TCP.
  • Unreliable:
  • Sender is not told.
  • Used when some loss is acceptable, e.g. video.
  • E.g. IP and UDP.
71
Reliable: the sender is told what arrived (TCP). Unreliable: the sender is not told (UDP, IP).

14.6 Transmission Control
Protocol

  • Passes data between applications and IP.
  • Connection-oriented.
  • Handshake: request, acknowledgement, acknowledgement.
  • Two-way (duplex) connection.
  • Splits data into numbered segments.
  • Sequence numbers put data back in order.
  • Checksums detect errors.
  • Missing or damaged packets are re-sent.
72
The three-way handshake, sequence numbers and re-sending. Demonstrate on the next slide.

14.6 Reliable & Unreliable

TCP or UDP: what happens when packets get lost?Set how many packets the network loses, then send 8 packets with each protocol.

TCP is reliable: the sender is told what arrived. UDP is unreliable: the sender is never told.
Try it
Set the loss to 25%. Run TCP and point out the handshake, the ACKs and the re-sends. Run UDP and point out the missing packets. Compare the times. Set the loss to 0% and repeat.

14.6 Internet Protocol (IP)

  • IP specifies:
  • The addressing system for packets
  • How packets are structured
  • How packets are fragmented and reassembled
  • Each device has a unique IP address.
  • Connectionless: no fixed route.
  • Routed from node to node to the destination.
  • Unreliable: sender not told of losses.
73
IP handles addressing and routing. It is connectionless and unreliable, which is why TCP is added on top.

14.6 ICMP, ARP & InARP

  • ICMP:
  • Sends error messages, not user data.
  • E.g. packet undeliverable or TTL expired.
  • Used by ping and traceroute.
  • ARP: finds a MAC address from an IP address.
  • Each device keeps an ARP list.
  • Replaced by Neighbour Discovery in IPv6.
  • InARP: finds an IP address from a MAC address.
74
ICMP: error messages (ping). ARP: IP → MAC. InARP: MAC → IP.

14.6 DHCP & UDP

  • DHCP:
  • Assigns IP addresses to devices automatically.
  • Also gives the default gateway address.
  • Address is leased and can be reassigned.
  • UDP:
  • Connectionless; no error checking.
  • Fast, so used for streaming and VoIP.
  • Used by DHCP, DNS lookups and SNMP.
75
DHCP leases IP addresses automatically. UDP is fast with no error checking, so it suits streaming and DNS.

14.6 HTTP & HTTPS

  • HTTP transfers web pages between server and browser.
  • Application-layer, request-response protocol.
  • Runs over TCP on port 80 or 8080.
  • Resources found by their URL.
  • HTTPS adds a TLS/SSL layer.
  • Encrypts requests and responses.
  • Authenticates the server with a digital certificate.
76
HTTP on port 80. HTTPS adds TLS: encryption plus server authentication with a certificate. Look for the padlock.

14.6 File Transfer Protocol
(FTP)

  • Transfers files between a client and an FTP server.
  • Control connection on port 21.
  • Active mode: server opens the data connection.
  • Passive mode: client opens the data connection.
  • Firewalls often block active mode.
  • Logins and data sent as plain text.
  • FTPS adds TLS encryption.
  • SFTP uses SSH instead.
77
FTP ports 21 and 20, active vs passive mode. Plain-text logins are a security risk.

14.6 Email Protocols

  • SMTP: sends email.
  • Client to server, and server to server.
  • Ports 587 and 25.
  • POP3: retrieves email; port 110.
  • Downloads, then deletes from the server.
  • IMAP: retrieves email; port 993 with TLS.
  • Leaves mail on the server.
  • Several devices can access one mailbox.
78
SMTP sends (ports 587/25). POP3 (110) downloads and deletes. IMAP (993) keeps mail on the server.

14.6 Telnet & SSH

  • Telnet:
  • Remote login to a host, e.g. a router.
  • Used for configuration and diagnosis.
  • Unencrypted, with almost unrestricted access.
  • Secure Shell (SSH):
  • Secure replacement for Telnet.
  • Public-key encryption authenticates both ends.
  • Used to manage servers and transfer files.
79
Telnet is unencrypted. SSH replaced it, using public-key encryption.

14.6 L2TP, IPsec & TLS

  • L2TP: tunneling protocol.
  • Creates the tunnel but doesn’t encrypt.
  • Lets packets cross different networks; supports VPNs.
  • IPsec: authenticates and encrypts IP packets.
  • Can wrap a whole packet, creating a VPN.
  • TLS (replaced SSL):
  • Public keys set up the connection.
  • Shared session keys then encrypt the data.
80
L2TP tunnels but does not encrypt, so it is paired with IPsec. TLS uses public keys, then shared session keys.

14.6 Packet Switching

  • Data split into small packets.
  • Each packet has source and destination addresses.
  • Packets may take different routes.
  • Routers forward each packet independently.
  • Packets reordered at the destination.
  • Interleaved with other traffic.
  • Efficient use of channels.
  • E.g. the internet.
81
Packets take independent routes and are reordered at the destination. The next slide shows it live.

14.6 Packet Switching

Packets take different routes and get put back in orderType a message and send it. Tap a router to switch it off. Tap a packet to read its header.

Each packet carries a sequence number, so the receiver can rebuild the message.
Try it
Send the default message and point out the different coloured routes and the arrival order. Switch off R4, then R1 and R2 together, to show re-routing and failure. Tap a packet to see its header.

14.6 Structure of a Packet

  • Header:
  • Source and destination IP addresses
  • Sequence number, protocol and TTL (hop count)
  • Checksum for the header
  • Payload: the actual data.
  • Trailer: end-of-packet flag and error check.
  • IP packets travel inside Ethernet frames.
  • Frames must not exceed the MTU.
82
Header, payload, trailer. TTL is the hop count. Frames must not exceed the MTU.

14.6 IPv4 & IPv6 Packets

  • IPv4 header:
  • 14 fields, 160–480 bits.
  • Includes a header checksum.
  • IPv6 header:
  • Fixed size of 320 bits.
  • Two 128-bit address fields.
  • No checksum.
  • Routers drop, not fragment, oversized packets.
83
IPv4 header 160–480 bits with a checksum. IPv6 is fixed at 320 bits with no checksum.

14.6 TCP & UDP Packets

  • TCP header:
  • Source and destination ports
  • Sequence and acknowledgement numbers
  • Flags, window size and checksum
  • UDP header: only 64 bits.
  • Source port, destination port, length, checksum
  • Port numbers identify the service.
  • E.g. 80 HTTP, 21 FTP, 67/68 DHCP.
84
Port numbers identify the service: 80 HTTP, 21 FTP, 67/68 DHCP. The UDP header is only 64 bits.

14.6 Modes of Connection

  • Connection-oriented (connection mode):
  • Link set up before data is sent.
  • Virtual circuit: all packets take one route.
  • Packets arrive in order; reliable.
  • E.g. frame relay and TCP.
  • Connectionless (datagram) mode:
  • No set-up; each packet routed separately.
  • E.g. Ethernet, IP and UDP.
85
Connection-oriented (a virtual circuit, in order) vs connectionless (datagrams, separate routes).

14.6 Frame Relay

  • Connection-oriented protocol at the Data Link layer.
  • Carries frames over public telecoms systems.
  • Each connection gets a virtual circuit identifier.
  • Permanent (PVC) or switched (SVC) circuits.
  • Variable-size frames.

Advantages

  • Fast; supports quality of service.

Disadvantages

  • No error correction; bad frames dropped.
  • End devices must handle errors.
86
Frame relay: fast and connection-oriented, but no error correction. PVC vs SVC.

14.6 Circuit Switching

  • Dedicated path set up before sending.
  • All data follows the same path.
  • Path released when transfer ends.
  • Used by traditional telephone calls.
  • Modern circuits are virtual, set by routers.

Advantages

  • Full bandwidth of the channel.

Disadvantages

  • Channel reserved even when idle.
  • Inefficient use of the network.
87
Circuit switching: a dedicated path, like a traditional phone call. Inefficient when idle.

14.6 Communication
Channels

  • Channel: pathway for data along a medium.
  • Can be physical, e.g. a copper wire.
  • Or logical, sharing one medium (multiplexing).
  • Time-division: channels take turns.
  • Up to 30 voice calls on one line.
  • Wave-division: each light wavelength is a channel.
  • Allows duplex communication along fibre.
88
Multiplexing shares one medium: time-division takes turns, wave-division uses different colours of light.

14.6 Message Switching

  • Whole message sent in one go.
  • Message carries addresses and error checks.
  • Store and forward at each node.
  • Each node receives, stores and checks it.
  • Then decides the next path.

Advantages

  • Can broadcast or prioritise messages.
  • Messages stored during congestion.

Disadvantages

  • Long delays; e.g. email servers.
89
Message switching: store and forward the whole message, as email servers do. Long delays.

14.6 MAC Addresses

  • Unique 48-bit address of a NIC.
  • Set during manufacture in ROM.
  • Six pairs of hex digits, e.g. 00-1A-2B-3C-4D-5E.
  • Half identifies the manufacturer.
  • Half identifies the individual NIC.
  • Used only within the same network.
  • Used by switches and by WAP allow lists.
  • DHCP uses it to assign IP addresses.
90
MAC address: 48 bits, in hex. Half identifies the manufacturer, half the NIC. Used only within the same network.

14.6 IPv4 Addresses

  • 32 bits in four 8-bit octets.
  • Written in decimal, e.g. 192.168.10.11.
  • Each octet is 0 to 255.
  • About 4.3 billion addresses.
  • Network part, e.g. 192.168.10.
  • Host part, e.g. .11.
  • Devices must share the network part to communicate.
  • Static or dynamic (assigned by DHCP).
91
32 bits, four octets. Network part vs host part. The next slide practises binary.

14.6 IPv4 Addresses

An IPv4 address is 32 bitsTap the bits, or type a number from 0 to 255 in each octet. Choose how many bits are the network part.

Network part
Host part
Hosts per network
All IPv4 addresses2³² ≈ 4.3 billion
Network part:
Each octet has 8 bits, worth 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2 and 1.
Try it
Run a few challenges with the class: students call out which bits to tap. Switch between /24 and /16 and compare the hosts per network.

14.6 IPv6 Addresses

  • 128 bits: vastly more addresses.
  • Eight groups of four hex digits.
  • Separated by colons, e.g. af33:9ffb:…
  • Network part is called the routing prefix.
  • Devices can configure their own addresses.
  • IPv4 and IPv6 are not interchangeable.
  • Tunneling carries one inside the other.
  • Dual stack: a device has both addresses.
92
IPv6 has 128 bits, written in hex with colons. Dual stack and tunneling help the transition.

14.6 Routing & Routing
Tables

  • Routing: finding a path for packets.
  • Three parts:
  • Routing protocols share network information.
  • Routing algorithms find paths.
  • Routing tables store the paths.
  • Every device has a routing table.
  • Unknown destination: sent to the default route.
  • View it with route print.
93
Routing protocols share information, algorithms find paths, and tables store them. Try “route print” on a school PC.

14.6 Static & Dynamic
Routing

  • Static: paths set manually by an administrator.
  • Dynamic: router builds and updates its own table.
  • Routers share status with each other.

Advantages

  • Full control; low CPU use; no extra traffic.
  • Adapts to congestion and failed routers.

Disadvantages

  • No fault tolerance.
  • Mistakes break routing; slow to update.
  • More processing and network traffic.
94
Static: manual control but no fault tolerance. Dynamic: adapts, but adds processing and traffic.

14.6 Selecting a Path

  • 1 Router reads the destination address.
  • 2 Searches its routing table.
  • 3 Directly connected: forward it.
  • 4 Otherwise calculate a routing metric.
  • Metric uses bandwidth, latency, hop count, MTU.
  • Lowest metric is the best route.
  • Best route is fastest, not shortest.
  • Routers share route updates.
95
The lowest metric wins: the fastest route, not the shortest. The next slide proves it.

14.6 Selecting a Path

Fastest route, not shortest routeEach number is a link's routing metric (lower is faster). Tap a link to change its speed.

Lowest metric (chosen)
Fewest hops
Router A's routing table
Try it
Send A→G: it takes 4 hops (metric 8), not 2 hops (metric 20). Tap the D–G link until it is fibre (1) and watch the route change. Ask what happens if a link becomes congested.

14.6 Routing Protocols

  • Interior gateway protocols (IGP):
  • Routing within a network.
  • Link-state, e.g. OSPF.
  • Distance-vector, e.g. RIP (counts hops).
  • Exterior gateway protocols (EGP):
  • Routing between networks, using rules and policies.
  • Border gateway protocol (BGP):
  • Exchanges routes across the internet.
96
IGP within a network (OSPF, RIP). EGP between networks (BGP holds the internet together).

14.6 Protocol Layering

  • Protocols are grouped into layers.
  • Layers form a network (protocol) stack.
  • Each layer has one job.
  • Layers can be changed independently.
  • Sending: each layer wraps data and adds a header.
  • Receiving: each layer removes its header.
  • This is encapsulation.
  • Two models: TCP/IP and OSI.
97
Layers each do one job. Sending adds headers and receiving removes them. This is encapsulation.

14.6 Protocol Layering

Encapsulation: each layer wraps the dataSending adds a header at each layer. Receiving removes them in reverse order.

Try it
Step through slowly and ask “what does this layer add?” before each click. Use Play all for a recap.

14.6 TCP/IP Suite

  • Application: prepares data for software.
  • HTTP, FTP, SMTP, IMAP, DHCP
  • Transport: connections, ports, error control.
  • TCP, UDP
  • Internet: addressing and routing.
  • IP, ICMP
  • Link: frames between two hosts.
  • Ethernet, Wi-Fi, ARP
98
The four TCP/IP layers with example protocols. Mnemonic: All Teachers Inspire Learners.

14.6 OSI Model: Layers 7–4

  • 7 Application: interface with user software.
  • 6 Presentation: formats, encrypts and compresses.
  • Decrypts and converts received data.
  • 5 Session: opens, manages and closes connections.
  • Checkpoints allow recovery.
  • 4 Transport: reliable delivery, segments.
  • Error checking and retransmission.
  • TCP, UDP and TLS.
99
OSI layers 7–4. Mnemonic for all seven, top down: All People Seem To Need Data Processing.

14.6 OSI Model: Layers 3–1

  • 3 Network: addressing and routing packets.
  • IP, ICMP; routers work here.
  • 2 Data Link: frames between nodes.
  • Maps IP to MAC addresses; switches work here.
  • 1 Physical: frames into signals.
  • Voltages, light pulses or radio waves.
  • Cables, connectors and pins.
100
OSI layers 3–1. Routers work at layer 3 and switches at layer 2.

14.6 TCP/IP vs OSI

  • Similarities:
  • Both are layered models.
  • Both have Application and Transport layers.
  • Both set standards so devices interoperate.
  • Differences:
  • TCP/IP has 4 layers; OSI has 7.
  • TCP/IP Application = OSI layers 7, 6 and 5.
  • TCP/IP is the practical standard.
101
TCP/IP has 4 layers and OSI has 7. TCP/IP Application = OSI layers 7, 6 and 5.

14.6 Firewalls

  • Barrier between networks, or on one host.
  • Hardware or software.
  • Monitors incoming and outgoing traffic.
  • Packet filtering: allow or block each packet.
  • Rules in access control lists (ACLs).
  • ACLs list IP addresses and port numbers.
  • Common rule: allow list, then deny all.
  • Unused ports should be closed.
102
Packet filtering with ACLs: allow a list, then deny all. Close unused ports.

14.6 Firewalls

Can you configure the firewall?Let customers and email in, and keep attackers out. Rules are checked from top to bottom, and the first match wins.

Access control list (ACL)
–good traffic let in
–attacks blocked
This firewall has some bad rules. Run the traffic, then fix the rules.
Try it
Run the traffic with the default rules and discuss the score. Fix one rule at a time with the class: turn off Telnet, add email, block the attacker, then DENY ALL.

14.6 Firewall Zones & the
DMZ

  • Firewalls can separate network zones.
  • E.g. servers, users and private databases.
  • DMZ: section reachable from the internet.
  • Holds web, email, FTP and VoIP servers.
  • Created between two firewalls.
  • External firewall faces the internet.
  • Internal firewall protects the company LAN.
  • Confidential databases never go in the DMZ.
103
The DMZ sits between two firewalls and holds public servers. Confidential databases never go in it.

14.6 Mind Map

Protocols, addressing & routing: the big pictureTap a branch to focus on it. Tap ↗ to jump to that slide.

Summary
Use this to recap the section. Ask students to explain one branch each, or tap a branch to jump back to its slide.

14.6 Quick Quiz

Quiz
This is the biggest section, so it has 6 questions. Revisit packet switching or routing if students struggle.

PAST PAPERSMARK SCHEME

104–105
Give students a few minutes to answer, then press Reveal mark scheme and self-mark.

14.7 Wireless Technology

  • Data carried by electromagnetic waves.
  • No cable guides the signal.
  • Methods:
  • Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and NFC
  • Infrared, microwave and radio
  • Uses:
  • Data exchange and mobile communications
  • Connecting the Internet of Things (IoT)
106
Wireless means electromagnetic waves with no cable. Preview the methods covered.

14.7 Wi-Fi

  • Wireless LAN protocols (IEEE 802.11).
  • Uses the 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz bands.
  • 2.4 GHz: longer range, less bandwidth.
  • 5 GHz: more bandwidth, shorter range.
  • Bands divided into channels.
  • Low power: limited range through walls.
  • Frames carry MAC addresses and the SSID.
  • Infrastructure mode via a WAP, or ad hoc.
107
2.4 GHz has more range; 5 GHz has more bandwidth. Ask which band works better through walls.

14.7 Wi-Fi: Evaluation

Advantages

  • Connect from anywhere in range.
  • Free public hotspots in cafes and hotels.
  • Easy to add smart devices at home.
  • VoIP calls where mobile signal is poor.

Disadvantages

  • Limited range; blocked by walls.
  • Interference from other radio devices.
  • Shared bands, so congestion.
  • Less secure than a wired connection.
108
Wi-Fi evaluation. Link the disadvantages to the security issues later in this section.

14.7 Bluetooth

  • Short-range radio in the 2.4 GHz band.
  • Range about 10 m; up to 8 devices.
  • Devices scan, then pair, often with a code.
  • Frequency hopping across 79 channels.
  • Piconet: small ad hoc network.
  • Scatternet: linked piconets.
  • E.g. headsets, keyboards, car hands-free.
  • Has its own protocol stack.
109
Bluetooth: about 10 m, 8 devices, pairing, frequency hopping. Piconet vs scatternet.

14.7 Bluetooth: Evaluation

Advantages

  • Simple set-up; reconnects automatically.
  • Low power, so long battery life.
  • Usually encrypted.
  • Short range makes eavesdropping harder.

Disadvantages

  • Short range.
  • Low bandwidth, so slow transfers.
  • Open connections can leak personal data.
110
Low power and short range are both a strength and a weakness.

14.7 Infrared

  • Light just beyond red in the spectrum.
  • Data sent as pulses of IR.
  • Needs line of sight; blocked by walls.
  • E.g. TV remote controls.
  • IR lasers link buildings at about 4 Gbit/s.

Advantages

  • Cheap, low power, no radio interference.

Disadvantages

  • Short range and low bandwidth.
  • Devices can’t move during transfer.
111
Infrared needs line of sight. Demonstrate with a TV remote: cover it with your hand.

14.7 Microwave

  • Short radio waves; travel in straight lines.
  • Line of sight only.
  • Relay stations about 70 km apart.
  • Directional antennae on tall towers.
  • Used by Wi-Fi, satellites and TV outside broadcasts.

Advantages

  • High bandwidth over long distances.

Disadvantages

  • Blocked by hills, buildings and trees.
  • Weakened by rain, snow and solar activity.
112
Microwave towers relay about 70 km apart. Weather and hills block the signal.

14.7 Radio

  • Waves longer than infrared.
  • Carries Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and mobile signals.
  • Very long waves pass through sea water.
  • Used to reach submarines, with tiny bandwidth.
  • Higher frequency: more bandwidth, shorter range.

Advantages

  • Long range; no cables to install.

Disadvantages

  • Blocked or absorbed by objects.
113
Radio: long range. Very long waves even reach submarines, with tiny bandwidth.

14.7 Near Field
Communication (NFC)

  • Very short range: about 10 cm.
  • Slow: up to 424 kbit/s.
  • Connects with one tap; no passwords.
  • Short range makes it secure.
  • Contactless payments and smart cards.
  • Share contacts, photos and links.
  • ‘Bootstraps’ Bluetooth or Wi-Fi connections.
  • Healthcare: tags track patients and drugs.
114
NFC works at about 10 cm with one tap. Ask who pays with their phone.

14.7 Wireless Power
Transfer

  • Electromagnetic waves carry energy.
  • Energy turned into DC electricity.
  • Charging pads need close contact.
  • Wi-Fi, 4G and 5G signals charge from further away.
  • Powers IoT devices in hard-to-reach places.
  • Could power implants, e.g. pacemakers.
  • Convenient and safe; no cables.
115
Wireless charging. Future: powering medical implants.

14.7 Wireless: Evaluation

Advantages

  • Users move freely while connected.
  • Less cabling, so cheaper to install.
  • Works where wiring isn’t allowed.
  • Devices easily added or removed.

Disadvantages

  • Shorter range than wired.
  • Lower bandwidth; less reliable.
  • Less control over connecting devices.
  • Signals can be intercepted outside the building.
116
Wireless overall: freedom vs range, bandwidth and security.

14.7 Wireless Security
Issues

  • Signals spread beyond the building.
  • Eavesdroppers can capture data.
  • Not all wireless data is encrypted.
  • Fake WAP: man-in-the-middle attack.
  • Public hotspots are often unencrypted.
  • Laptops can be turned into rogue WAPs.
  • Prevention: VPNs, HTTPS and strong passphrases.
  • Separate guest networks for visitors.
117
Fake WAPs are a man-in-the-middle attack. Advice: use a VPN on public Wi-Fi.

14.7 WEP & WPA

  • WEP (Wired Equivalent Privacy):
  • Fixed 64- or 128-bit keys.
  • Keys easily cracked; no longer used.
  • WPA (Wi-Fi Protected Access):
  • TKIP uses new keys for each packet.
  • Message integrity check detects changes.
  • WPA2 and WPA3 use longer keys.
  • WPS PINs open to brute force attacks.
118
WEP is broken. WPA uses TKIP with per-packet keys. Use WPA2 or WPA3. WPS PINs can be brute-forced.

Wireless technology: the big pictureTap a branch to focus on it. Tap ↗ to jump to that slide.

Use this to recap the section. Ask students to explain one branch each, or tap a branch to jump back to its slide.

14.7 Quick Quiz

Quiz
Students answer, then read the explanation. Use “Try again” for a second attempt; the options are reshuffled.

PAST PAPERSMARK SCHEME

119–120
Give students a few minutes to answer, then press Reveal mark scheme and self-mark.

14.8 Cellular Networks

  • Area split into cells, roughly hexagonal.
  • Base station at the centre of each cell.
  • Antenna, transmitter, receiver and control unit.
  • Low power, short range.
  • Each cell has 10–50 frequencies.
  • Adjacent cells use different frequencies.
  • Base stations link to public telecoms.
  • Cities need many small cells.
121
Cells are roughly hexagonal with a base station in each. Cities need many small cells.

14.8 Frequency Reuse &
Handoff

  • Limited number of radio frequencies.
  • Distant cells reuse the same frequencies.
  • Low power stops interference between cells.
  • Multiplexing shares channels between users.
  • Handoff: call passed to the next base station.
  • Phone switches frequency automatically.
  • User notices no interruption.
  • Roaming: guest on another provider’s network.
122
Frequency reuse and handoff. The next slide lets students drive through the cells.

14.8 Frequency Reuse
& Handoff

Moving between cellsDrag the phone, or tap anywhere on the map. Colours show frequencies, and neighbouring cells never share one.

Connected to–
Frequency–
Signal
Handoffs0
The phone connects to its nearest base station.
Try it
Press “Take a drive” and count the handoffs. Toggle frequency reuse to see the same-coloured cells. Compare 3 and 7 frequencies: more frequencies means less interference but fewer channels per cell.

14.8 3G, 4G & 5G

  • 3G: GPRS data; circuit and packet switching.
  • About 2 Mbit/s fixed, far less when moving.
  • 4G: all-IP packet switching.
  • Up to 1 Gbit/s; streams HD video.
  • More users and better roaming.
  • 5G: higher frequencies; very small cells.
  • About 500 Mbit/s typical; very low latency.
  • Remote surgery, IoT and smart cars.
123
3G GPRS, 4G all-IP, 5G with very low latency. Ask what 5G enables, e.g. remote surgery.

14.8 Mobile Hotspots

  • Phone shares its 4G or 5G connection.
  • Other devices connect by Wi-Fi.

Advantages

  • Secure, private connection.
  • Works anywhere with a mobile signal.
  • No need to find public Wi-Fi.

Disadvantages

  • Bandwidth shared between devices.
  • Extra charges or data limits.
  • Drains the phone’s battery.
124
Hotspot: the phone shares its mobile data over Wi-Fi. Mention data limits and battery drain.

14.8 Satellite
Communications

  • Satellites relay data around the world.
  • Uplink: ground station to satellite.
  • Downlink: satellite to ground station.
  • Needs line of sight.
  • Geostationary satellites stay over one point.
  • Low-orbit satellites need constellations.
  • Used for internet, TV, radio and telephones.
  • Also ATMs, EPOS and weather data.
125
Uplink and downlink. Geostationary satellites stay over one point; low-orbit satellites work in constellations.

14.8 Sending Data by
Satellite

  • 1 Data arrives at the ground station.
  • 2 Modulated onto uplink microwave frequencies.
  • 3 Dish aimed precisely at the satellite.
  • 4 Transponder changes the frequency.
  • 5 Data sent down on the downlink frequency.
  • 6 Ground station demodulates the data.
  • 7 Data sent on to the recipient.
  • Uplink power is higher than downlink.
126
Seven steps of satellite transmission. The transponder changes the frequency.

14.8 Global Positioning
System

  • 31 satellites at about 22 200 km.
  • Receivers only receive; they don’t transmit.
  • Needs at least 4 satellites for accuracy.
  • Uses signal timings to calculate distances.
  • Trilateration gives latitude, longitude and altitude.
  • Location shown on stored maps.
  • Mobile data adds traffic and weather updates.
127
GPS receivers only receive. Distance = time × speed of light. Trilateration. At least 4 satellites.

14.8 Global Positioning System

How does a GPS receiver find itself?Drag the phone. Each satellite's signal time gives a distance, a circle. Where do the circles meet?

Position?
Satellites:
Try it
Start with 1 satellite (a circle), then 2 (two points), then 3 (one point). Turn on the clock error and the circles miss. Add the 4th satellite to fix it.

14.8 Uses of GPS

  • Aviation: flight plans and tracking.
  • Shipping, fishing and port navigation.
  • Mining and construction machinery.
  • Taxis, deliveries and emergency vehicles.
  • Fitness, hiking and photo tagging.
  • Active tracking: real time via mobile data.
  • Passive tracking: stored, downloaded later.
  • Drones, robots and animal tracking.
128
Uses of GPS. Active tracking (real time) vs passive tracking (downloaded later).

14.8 Mapping &
Surveillance

  • Global mapping:
  • Earth observation satellites photograph the surface.
  • Used for maps, e.g. Google Maps.
  • Monitors climate, crops and glaciers.
  • Surveillance:
  • Governments watch other countries.
  • Police track criminals and terrorists.
  • Raises privacy concerns.
129
Mapping and surveillance. Discuss the privacy concerns.

14.8 Satellite Internet, TV &
Phones

  • Internet: remote areas, ships and aircraft.
  • High latency, about 550 ms or more.
  • Delays can break secure connections.
  • TV: broadcast direct to home dishes.
  • LNB converts signals for coaxial cable.
  • Encryption controls paid channels.
  • Satphones: calls from almost anywhere.
  • Weather can weaken signals.
130
Satellite internet: about 550 ms of latency. Ask why that is a problem for online gaming.

14.9 Network Security
Threats

  • Network data is shared, so vulnerable.
  • Threats:
  • Brute force and denial of service (DoS)
  • Botnets and malware
  • Malicious actors
  • SQL injection
  • Poor network policies
  • Hacking: access without the usual credentials.
133
An overview of threats. Each is covered on the next slides.

14.9 Brute Force & DoS

  • Brute force: tries many passwords.
  • Often automated; fast on short passwords.
  • Prevent: long passwords, lockouts, MFA, CAPTCHA.
  • Denial of service (DoS):
  • Floods a server with requests.
  • Legitimate users can’t access it.
  • Distributed DoS uses many attacking devices.
  • Prevent: firewall rules, scrubbing centres.
134
Brute force and DoS. Use the next slide to show why long passwords matter.

14.9 Brute Force & DoS

How long would a brute-force attack take?Type a made-up password (never a real one). The attacker tries every combination.

Attacker:
Attacker's screen
········
Press ▶ Attack
Time to try every combination
Try it
Try “cat123” (cracked instantly), then add capitals, symbols and length. Switch the attacker speed. Turn on lockout with the online attacker. Remind students never to type a real password.

14.9 Botnets

  • Network of infected devices (bots).
  • Bot installed without the owner knowing.
  • Controlled by a bot herder.
  • Command and control server, or peer-to-peer.
  • Used for DDoS attacks.
  • Sends spam and phishing emails.
  • Spyware and keyloggers harvest credentials.
  • Uses the victim’s resources, e.g. mining Bitcoin.
135
Botnets: infected “zombie” devices controlled by a bot herder. Used for DDoS, spam and crypto-mining.

14.9 Malware

  • Software designed to cause damage.
  • Viruses, worms, Trojans, spyware, adware.
  • Exploits software flaws and careless users.
  • Spreads by email, downloads and networks.
  • Deletes, manipulates, modifies or steals data.
  • Ransomware encrypts data and demands payment.
  • Shared cloud servers spread attacks.
136
Types of malware. Ransomware: paying is no guarantee you get your data back.

14.9 Malicious Actors &
SQL Injection

  • Malicious actors: people who harm systems.
  • Cybercriminals: money.
  • State agencies: spying.
  • Insiders and competitors: business advantage.
  • SQL injection:
  • Malicious SQL typed into web forms.
  • Reveals passwords and card details.
  • Prevent: least privilege, fixed SQL, updates.
137
Malicious actors and their motives. SQL injection: typing code into forms.

14.9 Network Policies

  • Rules for how the network is used.
  • Technologies allowed, e.g. USB sticks.
  • Acceptable use policy.
  • Users’ responsibilities and breach reporting.
  • Password policy and security protocols.
  • Staff sign non-disclosure agreements.
  • Basis for legal action if broken.
  • Poor policies leave the network open.
138
Network policies, e.g. the school’s acceptable use policy. Ask: what does ours say?

14.9 Impact: Destruction &
Manipulation

  • Data destruction:
  • Lost orders, customer data or photos.
  • Ransom may be paid, with no guarantee.
  • Firms can go out of business.
  • Data manipulation:
  • Data presented in a misleading way.
  • Victims doubt their own data.
  • Damages reputations and influences elections.
139
Impact: destruction and manipulation.

14.9 Impact: Modification &
Theft

  • Modification: the data itself is changed.
  • Often by insiders.
  • Wrong medical records can harm patients.
  • Hard to detect and costly to correct.
  • Theft of data:
  • Fraud with stolen card details.
  • Fines, lawsuits and lost customers.
  • Breaches must be reported to those affected.
140
Modification (often by insiders) and theft. Breaches must be reported.

14.9 Impact: Identity Theft

  • Using another person’s identity.
  • Uses names, dates of birth, passport numbers.
  • Gathered from social media, spyware, botnets.
  • Buy goods or open accounts in their name.
  • Victim’s credit rating is damaged.
  • Identity cloning: living as someone else.
  • Can take years to put right.
141
Identity theft can take years to put right. Advice: limit what you share on social media.

14.9 Physical Prevention

  • Locked doors to server rooms.
  • Barriers and turnstiles at entrances.
  • Security guards check credentials.
  • CCTV monitored, with alarms.
  • Smartcards, PINs and RFID for doors.
  • Cable locks; USB ports removed.
  • Air gap: no connection to other networks.
  • Shred confidential paper waste.
142
Physical prevention, from locks to air gaps. Spot the measures used around the school.

14.9 Biometrics

  • Unique body characteristics.
  • E.g. fingerprints, iris, retina, face, palm.
  • Enrolment: data stored as templates.
  • Reading compared with stored templates.
  • Match within a margin of error grants access.
  • Often combined with a PIN or card.
  • Zero-login: biometrics replace passwords.
143
Biometrics: enrolment, then matching against templates within a margin of error.

14.9 Anti-Malware Software

  • Scans files against databases of known malware.
  • Heuristics spot malware-like behaviour.
  • Quarantines or deletes suspicious files.
  • Monitors network entry points.
  • Sandboxing: malware analysed in isolation.
  • Anti-virus: stops self-copying viruses.
  • Anti-spyware: stops hidden tracking software.
  • Must be kept up to date.
144
Signature scanning vs heuristics. It must be kept up to date.

14.9 Encryption

  • Turns data into unintelligible ciphertext.
  • Symmetric: same key encrypts and decrypts.
  • Asymmetric: public key encrypts, private key decrypts.
  • Asymmetric used to share symmetric keys.
  • Used by TLS, VPNs and Wi-Fi.
  • Digital certificates prove a site is genuine.
  • Issued by certificate authorities.
  • Stolen data is useless without the key.
145
Symmetric vs asymmetric encryption. The next slide demonstrates both.

14.9 Encryption

Symmetric encryption: the same key locks and unlocksA Caesar cipher shifts each letter by the key. Try to crack it.

Try it
Symmetric: encrypt a message, then press Crack it to show why 25 keys is weak. Asymmetric: step through the padlock story, and stress that Eve sees everything but cannot open the box.

14.9 Access Rights

  • Control who can view, change or run files.
  • File permissions:
  • Read only
  • Read and write
  • Execute
  • Set for users or groups.
  • Hidden folders for unauthorised users.
  • E.g. data entry, but no exporting.
146
Read, write, execute. Least privilege.

14.9 Evaluation: Physical &
Biometric

Advantages

  • Physical: stops direct access to hardware.
  • Biometrics can’t be forgotten or shared.
  • Hard to forge; fast to use.

Disadvantages

  • Keys lost or copied; guards can be bribed.
  • CCTV raises privacy concerns.
  • Expensive; false positives and negatives.
  • Unhygienic; injuries change fingerprints.
  • Biometric data must be protected.
147
Evaluate physical and biometric methods. False positives vs false negatives.

14.9 Evaluation: Software
Methods

Advantages

  • Anti-malware scans in real time.
  • Encryption protects data anywhere.
  • Access rights stop careless mistakes.
  • Firewalls block threats before entry.

Disadvantages

  • Slows systems; misses brand new malware.
  • Lost keys mean lost data.
  • Complex to configure.
  • Firewalls slow traffic and restrict staff.
148
Evaluate software methods. Every method has a trade-off.

149–150

14.10 Disaster-Recovery
Management

  • Disaster: damage to IT systems or services.
  • Causes:
  • Natural disasters, e.g. floods, fires
  • Equipment and power failures
  • Cybercrime, malware and criminal activity
  • Accidents, e.g. deleted files
  • Plan: prevent, detect, recover.
  • Restores services in the shortest time.
151
A disaster-recovery plan: prevent, detect, recover. List the causes.

14.10 Threats, Risks &
Vulnerabilities

  • Threat: factor that could harm IT services.
  • Risk: possibility of harm happening.
  • Vulnerability: weakness an attacker can exploit.
  • E.g. staff not logging out.
  • Types of threat:
  • Technical, e.g. power cuts, overheating
  • Human, e.g. malware, accidental deletion
  • Physical and environmental, e.g. theft, flood
152
Threat vs risk vs vulnerability: a common exam question.

14.10 Risk Analysis

  • Also called a risk assessment.
  • Identify the possible threats.
  • Assess the vulnerability to each.
  • Judge how likely each threat is.
  • Decide who or what would carry it out.
  • Consider the cost of prevention.
  • Decide control measures.
153
Steps of a risk assessment.

14.10 Perpetrator Analysis

  • Perpetrator: person who causes harm.
  • Identifies likely attackers and their aims.
  • Script kiddie: uses others’ code to impress.
  • Cracker: exploits flaws; uses software without paying.
  • Also hackers, insiders, spies and cyberterrorists.
  • Banks attract financially motivated criminals.
  • Logs and traffic analysis reveal attackers.
154
Perpetrators: script kiddies, crackers, insiders and spies.

14.10 Risk Testing &
Quantifying

  • Risk testing:
  • Rehearse plans, e.g. restoring data.
  • Find the extent of each threat.
  • Quantifying the risk:
  • Risk matrix: likelihood against impact.
  • Rate risks low to extremely high.
  • Assign a monetary cost.
  • Combine experts’ scores.
155
Risk matrix: likelihood × impact.

14.10 Control of Threats

  • Mitigation reduces the damage of a threat.
  • Fire: detectors and suppression systems.
  • Unstable power: voltage regulators.
  • Overheating: air conditioning.
  • Lightning: grounding systems.
  • Accidents: policies, training and backups.
  • Strict controls can hinder staff.
156
Mitigation controls for each threat.

14.10 Detecting Threats

  • Alerts from firewalls and anti-malware.
  • Unusual activity, e.g. failed logins.
  • Signature-based: known attack patterns.
  • Behaviour baselines spot anomalies.
  • E.g. a login at 4 a.m. from abroad.
  • Traps lure intruders and raise alerts.
  • Intrusion detection at gateways and hosts.
  • Insider threats: large downloads, unusual access.
157
Signature-based vs behaviour-based detection. Example: a 4 a.m. login from abroad.

14.10 Restoring After a
Disaster

  • Follow the disaster-recovery plan.
  • Find and correct the cause.
  • Replace hardware; remove malware first.
  • Restore data from recent backups.
  • Mirror or virtual servers replace failed ones.
  • Cloud providers restore quickly.
  • Ransomware: restore backups; change passwords.
  • Test restores regularly.
158
Restore: fix the cause first, then restore the backups. Test restores regularly.

14.10 Protecting Power
Supplies

  • Power loss can lose data and damage disks.
  • Surges and voltage drops cause faults.
  • Journaling file systems help recovery.
  • Surge protectors stop power spikes.
  • Generators run during long power cuts.
  • UPS: batteries give instant backup power.
  • UPS allows a safe shutdown.
159
UPS for short gaps and safe shutdown, generators for long power cuts.

14.10 Passwords & Access
Control

  • Authentication: proving who you are.
  • Something you know, have or are.
  • Authorisation: what you can access.
  • Access control instructions per folder or file.
  • Audit: log of user activity.
  • Passwords on files keep them secure.
  • Forgotten keys or passwords lose data.
160
Authentication: something you know, have or are. Authorisation: what you can access.

14.10 Protection from
Malware & Access

  • Firewalls check packets at entry points.
  • Block insecure protocols, e.g. FTP.
  • Scan email attachments automatically.
  • Central security suite for large organisations.
  • Train staff to spot phishing.
  • Disable unused network services.
  • Home access only through a VPN.
  • Close unused ports; separate guest Wi-Fi.
161
Practical protection checklist.

14.10 Backup Strategies

  • What, how often, where and who.
  • Back up data, systems and configurations.
  • Store on NAS, SAN, cloud or off-site tape.
  • Keep backups disconnected from the network.
  • RPO: maximum acceptable data loss.
  • RTO: maximum time allowed for recovery.
  • MTD: longest tolerable downtime.
  • System image restores a whole disk.
162
RPO, RTO and MTD are often confused. Have students define each in their own words.

14.10 Backup Rotation

  • First in, first out (FIFO):
  • Several media sets used in turn.
  • Oldest set is overwritten next.
  • Grandfather-father-son (GFS):
  • Daily, weekly and monthly backups.
  • Tower of Hanoi: complex rotation.
  • Some sets removed and archived.
  • Store backups safely, away from originals.
163
FIFO vs GFS. The next slide shows why GFS keeps older restore points.

14.10 Backup Rotation

Which backups do you still have?Run three months of daily backups, then discover a virus that arrived three weeks ago.

Restore points you could go back to
Same five working days a week. Which strategy keeps older backups?
Try it
Run GFS, then the virus: you can restore from an older tape. Run FIFO, then the virus: every backup is infected. Ask: what is the trade-off? (More tapes and storage.)
